finding.claim: testBit() is off by one: it reads bit position-1, so inspectTeredo() reports the wrong Teredo flag bits (coneNat, reserved, groupIndividual, universalLocal). Example: the flags word 0x8000 (cone bit set) yields coneNat=false.
finding.source: Caller-supplied IPv6 address in 2001::/32, e.g. '2001:0:4136:e378:8000:63bf:3fff:fdd2' (flags group 0x8000). Input is not a security boundary here, so this is a correctness bug with no direct attacker control over the library's trust decisions.
finding.sink: inspectTeredo() return fields coneNat / reserved / microsoft.groupIndividual / microsoft.universalLocal (consumers that act on these flags).

trace.note: flagsBase2 = getBitsBase2(64,80): 16-char MSB-first string, index 0 = bit 15
guard: if (position > length) return false (should be >=)
positionInString = length - position = 1 for position 15; the correct index is length-1-position = 0
substring(1,2) returns bit 14 (the R bit), not the cone bit at index 0
reserved = testBit(...,14) therefore reads bit 13 (an A bit)
groupIndividual = testBit(...,8) reads bit 7 instead of bit 8 (G)
universalLocal = testBit(...,9) reads bit 8 (G) instead of bit 9 (U)

finding.guards_checked: Checked nonce (ipv6.ts:994, slices, correct) and udpPort (ipv6.ts:978-979, XOR, correct); prefix/server4/client4 are correct. Only the testBit-derived booleans are wrong. No validation exists to catch this. Repro: new Address6('2001:0:4136:e378:8000:63bf:3fff:fdd2').inspectTeredo().coneNat returns false; expected true.

finding.claim: href(optionalPort) concatenates the port argument into the URL without validation or escaping, so a string port can change the host of the returned HTTP URL (userinfo/host confusion).
finding.source: The optionalPort parameter, typed number | string (ipv6.ts:1446). Attacker-controlled only if a caller forwards untrusted input as the port.
finding.sink: The returned URL string, documented as an HTTP URL and likely used as an href or redirect target.

trace.note: optionalPort = `:${optionalPort}` with no check that it is numeric or in 0-65535

finding.guards_checked: The address part is safe because correctForm() yields only hex and colons. link() (ipv6.ts:1488-1489) escapes its output with escapeHtml, but that is HTML escaping, not URL validation, and href() has no equivalent. Repro: new Address6('2001:db8::1').href('1@evil.example') gives 'http://[2001:db8::1]:1@evil.example/', whose WHATWG host is evil.example. Severity low: it needs a caller that passes untrusted data as the port. Confidence: plausible.

finding.claim: isPrivate() and isLoopback() do not decode 6to4 (2002::/16) embedded IPv4 addresses, so an address whose 6to4 gateway field is an RFC 1918 or loopback IPv4 is classified as public.
finding.source: Attacker-supplied IPv6 literal, e.g. 2002:0a00:0001::1 (6to4 gateway 10.0.0.1). Used in an SSRF or trust-boundary filter that calls isPrivate()/isLoopback() on the destination.
finding.sink: Allow/deny decision on the destination address (protected operation: outbound connection to an internal host through a 6to4 relay).

trace.note: embeddedIPv4() returns an embedded address only for isMapped4() or NAT64_WELL_KNOWN; 6to4 is not handled
falls through to isULA() (fc00::/7: false) or NAT64_LOCAL_USE (false), so returns false
isLoopback() likewise returns getType()==='Loopback' (false), since getType gives '6to4' per constants.ts:51

finding.guards_checked: The documented scope at ipv6.ts:1295-1310 covers only mapped and NAT64 addresses, so this is a documented gap, not a logic slip. The 6to4 gateway field is decoded in inspect6to4() (ipv6.ts:1017-1031) but not used by the classifiers. Exploitability needs the network to route 2002::/16 through a 6to4 relay that reaches the embedded IPv4 host, which is uncommon. Severity low. Confidence: plausible.
